doc.title: Pierre Boussaguet interviewed by Matthieu Jaffre, Aix en Provence, France, July 28, 2020

title: Ray Brown's life lessons on the road and in the studio
summary: Brown teaches him about the business, about days off, and about studio professionalism by example.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Not in terms of negotiation or stuff like that but just to — one time — I will put it this way. One time we had an argument. And at some point I faced him and I said, “What do you expect from me?” I said, “I heard, you keep repeating that, I know what you’re talking about so tell me what should I do?” And he cracked up laughing and he said, with his cap he just banged me on the shoulder and he said, “I’m trying to help you. You and young musicians. I don’t want you, all of you guys, to do the same errors we did.
Exactly. Wow, that’s such a gift. And that’s being so intelligent.

See I don’t want you to — he learned me a lot of things. For instance, one time we were driving. I was doing the driving. We were playing that night, then dealing with the contracts, with everything. And just like that he gave me simple things. Then I remember

one time we had the day off, we traveled and we used that day to travel for five or six hours. And when we got there, we arrived in Switzerland I remember. It was like 3:30, 4 in the afternoon. And at that time he said, “What you doing?” I said, “Ah, I’m going to rest in my room.” He said, “No.” He said, “Look, it’s springtime, come on, let’s have a drink.” A drink at that time? He said —
No, no, he said, “This is your day off.”

You’ve been working hard for the past ten days, so if there is one day to have a nice scotch or a vodka or whatever, and an ice cream, that’s the moment. And then later on you go to bed and you rest. That type of things. But never, never with a preaching attitude. Just, it was —
It’s like today most of the knowledge, you can find everything you want in a book, which I’m not against, it’s great. We didn’t have that information. Today you can have it.

But what still you need is being around the people. Recording with Ray I was very observing — the way he arrives to the studio, what he does. I noted that he didn’t drink tons of coffee, or he didn’t smoke tons of cigarettes before recording.
Yes, and all these little things, oh, that’s the way to deal with it. How to read music.
So you learned by his behavior as daily life, yeah.
